evidence.claim: Two dead ends became a mountain crossing between Lincoln and Conway.
evidence.quote: after two dead-end stretches of road were linked, creating a connection between US 3 in Lincoln and NH 16 in Conway.

evidence.claim: The Kancamagus Highway climbs through hairpin turns, crosses a mountain pass and descends beside the Swift River toward Conway.
evidence.quote: Following a series of hairpin turns, NH 112 crosses the height of land at 2,855-foot (870 m) Kancamagus Pass and begins to descend along the Swift River

evidence.claim: This is the Lincoln-to-Conway portion of New Hampshire Route 112.
evidence.quote: The eastern portion of NH 112 is known as the  Kancamagus Highway, running 32 miles (51 km) through the White Mountains from Lincoln to Conway.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration lists the Kancamagus as a National Scenic Byway, highlighting overlooks, forest ecology and the Russell Colbath Historic Site.
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway • New Hampshire

evidence.claim: Hiking trails and six national forest campgrounds line the route, extending the journey beyond its roadside outlooks.
evidence.quote: There are six National Forest campground sites, along with numerous hiking trails.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service singles out the route’s fall foliage scenery.
evidence.quote: The Kancamagus Scenic Byway offers one of the most beautiful routes through New Hampshire's White Mountains, especially during the fall foliage season.

evidence.claim: The through road opened in August 1959, when two dead-end roads were joined to connect Lincoln and Conway.
evidence.quote: The Kancamagus Highway opened in August 1959, after two dead-end stretches of road were linked, creating a connection between US 3 in Lincoln and NH 16 in Conway.

evidence.claim: Pavement followed in 1964, and the first winter plowing came in 1966–67.
evidence.quote: the road was paved in 1964, and in the winter of 1966–67 it was plowed for the first time.

evidence.claim: The highway bears the name of Kancamagus, the last leader of the Penacook Confederacy.
evidence.quote: The highway is named after Kancamagus (pronounced "cain-kah-MAW-gus", "Fearless One"), third and final sagamore of the Penacook Confederacy

evidence.claim: Travel east from Lincoln beside the East Branch of the Pemigewasset River, then the Hancock Branch, before climbing the hairpins to Kancamagus Pass.
evidence.quote: following the East Branch of the Pemigewasset River for approximately 4 miles (6 km), then the Hancock Branch for another 8 miles (13 km), steadily ascending as it progresses eastward.

evidence.claim: On the descent, the Swift River leads into the broad Albany Intervale, then a narrow gorge and two sets of small waterfalls.
evidence.quote: flows east into a broad valley, surrounded by mountains, known as the Albany Intervale. Leaving the intervale, the river enters a narrow gorge, passing over two sets of small waterfalls

evidence.claim: Along the eastern stretch, the Russell-Colbath House records nineteenth-century settlement, and Albany’s covered bridge spans the river.
evidence.quote: At the Russell-Colbath House Historic Site (77.1), see how 19th-century settlers lived

evidence.claim: The highway leaves the national forest and ends at Main Street in Conway, west of downtown.
evidence.quote: Eventually the highway leaves the National Forest and enters the town of Conway, where it terminates at Main Street (NH 16 / NH 113) west of downtown.

evidence.claim: highlighting overlooks, forest ecology and the Russell Colbath Historic Site.
evidence.quote: filled with scenic areas and overlooks. Visit the Russell Colbath Historic Site, which offers colonial history, and explore the Forest Discovery Trail, which provides forest ecology experiences in a living classroom.

evidence.claim: Albany’s covered bridge spans the river.
evidence.quote: covered bridge that spans the Swift River just north of the Kancamagus Highway.

evidence.claim: The climb from Lincoln reaches its turning point at Kancamagus Pass: beyond the hairpins, the highway starts descending along the Swift River.
evidence.quote: Following a series of hairpin turns, NH 112 crosses the height of land at 2,855-foot (870 m) Kancamagus Pass and begins to descend along the Swift River

evidence.claim: There is a scenic outlook near the crest.
evidence.quote: Two scenic outlook sites are located along the Kancamagus Highway, including one from near the crest of Kancamagus Pass.

evidence.claim: The river below the eastern side rises here and flows toward the Saco at Conway.
evidence.quote: The Swift River rises in the township of Livermore, New Hampshire, on the eastern side of Kancamagus Pass

evidence.claim: On the western approach, the East Branch of the Pemigewasset belongs to a different river system, the Merrimack watershed.
evidence.quote: It is a tributary of the Pemigewasset River, part of the Merrimack River watershed.

evidence.claim: The tourism guide identifies nearby outlooks toward the Pemigewasset, the Osceola Range and Mount Hancock.
evidence.quote: those with views of the Pemigewasset (86.7), the Osceola Range (88.5), and Mt. Hancock (89.1).

evidence.claim: The road follows the Swift River for the remaining 21 miles toward Conway.
evidence.quote: begins to descend along the Swift River in the Saco River watershed, which it does for its remaining 21 miles (34 km).

evidence.claim: flows toward the Saco at Conway.
evidence.quote: continues east through the town of Albany to the Saco River at Conway.

evidence.claim: A central chimney, clapboard walls and a symmetrical front mark the Russell-Colbath House beside the highway.
evidence.quote: It is a 1+1⁄2-story wood-frame structure, with a gable roof, central chimney, and clapboarded exterior.  It has a symmetrical five-bay facade

evidence.claim: At the front door, sidelight windows and pilasters frame the entrance beneath a simple peaked top.
evidence.quote: a center entrance flanked by sidelight windows and pilasters, and topped by a simple peaked entablature.

evidence.claim: Thomas and Amzi Russell built the house in 1831–32.
evidence.quote: The house was built in 1831-32 by Thomas and Amzi Russell

evidence.claim: They operated a sawmill on Oliverian Brook and belonged to a farming and logging community in the valley.
evidence.quote: The Russells operated a sawmill on Oliverian Brook, and were part of a small farming and logging community in the immediate area

evidence.claim: Russell descendants owned the house until 1930; it later served as a summer residence before the Forest Service acquired it in 1961.
evidence.quote: The house was owned by Russell descendants until 1930, after which it was used for a time as a summer residence.  It was acquired by the Forest Service in 1961

evidence.claim: The tourism association identifies it as the area’s only remaining nineteenth-century homestead.
evidence.quote: the Russell-Colbath House is the only remaining 19th-century homestead in the area

evidence.claim: The house has clapboard siding, a central chimney and sidelight windows flanking its entrance.
evidence.quote: a center entrance flanked by sidelight windows and pilasters

evidence.claim: The house has clapboard siding, a central chimney
evidence.quote: with a gable roof, central chimney, and clapboarded exterior.

evidence.claim: The covered bridge at Albany spans 120 feet across the Swift River just north of the Kancamagus Highway.
evidence.quote: features a 120-foot (37 m) covered bridge that spans the Swift River just north of the Kancamagus Highway.

evidence.claim: The White Mountains tourism guide places a campground beside it and notes displays explaining covered-bridge construction.
evidence.quote: including one by the Albany Covered Bridge (70.6), which also has displays about building covered bridges

evidence.claim: The Swift continues east through Albany to meet the Saco River at Conway.
evidence.quote: continues east through the town of Albany to the Saco River at Conway.

flags: Pass elevation is omitted: 01 and tourism guide 25 give 2,855 feet, while Lincoln page 29 gives 2,860 feet.
Route lengths differ in scope: FHWA 30 lists the designated byway at 26.5 miles; Forest Service 00 describes 34 miles; 01 gives 32 miles Lincoln to Conway. No single corridor mileage is asserted.
Passaconaway’s settlement date is omitted: tourism guide 25 says about 1790; house page 17 describes failed settlements in 1805 and 1815 and Russell arrival in the 1820s.

No Tribal or primary historical source for Kancamagus is cached. The road article uses both Penacook and Pennacook; retained its Penacook Confederacy name, omitted the migration account and motive pending community-source review.
The old draft’s claim that the house is open is supported by tourism guide 25 and museum use by 17, but no current manager access page is cached; no interior visit is promised.
Albany Covered Bridge is shorter than 90 words because the cached site-specific evidence is thin. The guide’s nearby swimming recommendations conflict with Rocky Gorge page 18; neither is reused.
